title: Do We Need to Learn How to Listen?
author: Alex Quigley
summary: Alex Quigley argues that in an age of constant talk and instant communication, listening has become the neglected half of classroom communication and deserves the same explicit teaching that speaking and debating already receive. He traces his own shift from assuming listening is a 'natural' skill to recognising that active listening -- attending to peers, picking up non-verbal cues, and making inferences -- needs modelling and practice like any other skill. Quigley points out that only modern foreign language teaching routinely tests listening comprehension, leaving most subjects with passive audiences during presentations and debates. He offers a toolkit of concrete strategies, including ABC feedback (Agree, Build upon, Challenge), Cold Calling and Doug Lemov's 'Ratio' concept, and several structured note-taking methods, framing all of them as ways to keep every student mentally engaged rather than just the one currently speaking. The piece closes by rooting the argument in a century-old precedent, the 1921 Newbolt Report's call to teach listening alongside speaking and reading.
points: Quigley's central claim -- that listening is treated as natural rather than taught -- reframes a skill most teachers assume needs no explicit instruction as one requiring the same scaffolding as writing or speaking.
He identifies modern foreign languages as the only curriculum area that routinely assesses listening, implying other subjects have a structural gap in how they check for genuine engagement.
The ABC feedback model (Agree, Build upon, Challenge) is offered as a concrete scaffold that removes the 'dunno' get-out clause and forces active listening during class discussion.

Quigley links Cold Calling and Doug Lemov's 'Ratio' concept directly to listening instruction, arguing their popularity stems from maximising the number of students who must mentally engage, not just the one called on.

By quoting the 1921 Newbolt Report's call to practise 'the art of listening' alongside speaking and reading, Quigley positions his argument as recovering a century-old insight rather than proposing something new.
quotes: We are in an age of communication. We are connected more than ever before: with the ability to talk to friends and family across the world in an instant.
When we think of communication, we promote and prioritise talk. We celebrate speeches. We train pupils to debate and discuss.
In our age of mass, never-ending communication, listening may just be the lost art that we need, in the classroom and beyond.
Of course, very quickly I recognised that pupils needed training in ‘active listening’ – not just developing their ability to talk.
In one area of the school curriculum, it is routine to teach and assess listening to others: that is in modern foreign languages.
It is likely why Doug Lemov's concept of 'Ratio' has proven so popular - as it puts the emphasis on all pupils' maximising their mental efforts.
This simple scaffold helps eliminate the ‘dunno’ get out clause, whilst promoting more careful listening to one another.
Now, more than ever, active and precise listening strategies may be crucial to teach explicitly and to learn successfully.
